accepted.question_text: How can researchers train smaller and more efficient language models that serve as cost-effective alternatives to very large language models, especially for task-specific settings that do not require the full generality of larger models, and what roles should parameter-efficient fine-tuning, teacher-student transfer, and other forms of distillation play in building such smaller models from larger ones?

evidence.quote: However, those large models are costly and inefficient in several dimensions (e.g. high latency). In response to all of this, there is a current research trend to come up with Small Language Models (SLMs) as a cost-effective alternative to LLMs, particularly when used on specific tasks that might not require the full generality of larger models.

More generally, we should expect many research efforts in this area of how to train smaller and more efficient models. Techniques such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), teacher/student, and other forms of distillation – see section III-I – will continue to be used to build a smaller model out of larger ones.

accepted.question_text: Which post-attention or otherwise new architectural paradigms should replace or substantially extend Transformer-based large language models, and how can those architectures support longer context windows and more efficient processing of long-context prompts than standard attention-based models?

evidence.quote: Transformer blocks have been a crucial and constant part of most of current LLM frameworks, and it’s a big question mark how much longer this architecture will be in vogue, and what will be the next big architectural break-through in the field of deep learning (and NLP).

While all of those models are very competitive in terms of performance in leaderboards and efficiency, they also address an important challenge in more traditional attention-based architectures: the lack of support for larger context windows.

Attention-based models are highly inefficient for longer contexts and that is why we should expect more research in different mechanisms that enable processing longer contexts and generally come up with more efficient architectures.

accepted.question_text: How should future large language models be designed and evaluated so that they can handle text, images, video, and audio in a unified multi-modal manner for applications such as question answering, content generation, healthcare, robotics, and especially conversational generative vision?

evidence.quote: Future LLMs are expected to be multi-modal and handle a variety of data types, such as text, images, and videos, audio, in a unified manner. This opens up possibilities for more diverse applications in fields like question answering, content generation, creative arts, and healthcare, robotics, and beyond.
Evaluation of these models also is a new research topic, especially conversational generative vision models [217].

accepted.question_text: Which advanced prompt-engineering, tool-use, retrieval-augmentation, personalization, agent, and multi-agent techniques can most effectively address shortcomings of large language models such as hallucination while enabling systems that use external tools, incorporate user context, and make decisions in real applications?

evidence.quote: As we described in sectionIV, many of the shortcomings and limitations of LLMs such as hallucination can be addressed through advanced prompt engineering, use of tools, or other augmentation techniques. We should expect not only continued, but accelerated research in this area.
We will continue to see research in the application and usage of LLMs for not only personalization and recommendations, but many other application areas using other machine learning techniques.

Finally, another important area of research we expect to gather increased attention is that of LLM-based agents and multi-agent systems [172], [173], [174]. The development of LLM systems with access to external tools and decision-making capabilities is both exciting and challenging.

accepted.question_text: How can large language models be made robust and secure against adversarial attacks and other vulnerabilities, prevented from being used to manipulate people or spread misinformation, and improved so they better detect potential attacks while remaining fair, unbiased, and responsible with sensitive information?

evidence.quote: Ensuring the robustness and security of LLMs against adversarial attacks and other vulnerabilities is a critical area of research [219]. As LLMs are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, they need to be protected from potential threats, to prevent them being used to manipulate people or spread mis-information. Improving the reasoning capabilities of these model [220], would help them to better detect potential adversarial attacks.

Addressing ethical concerns and biases in LLMs is another active area of research. Efforts are being made to ensure that LLMs are fair, unbiased, and capable of handling sensitive information responsibly.

accepted.question_text: How can hallucination in large language models be measured reliably when the same factual content can be expressed in different styles and even very small wording changes make false-information detection difficult?

evidence.quote: Hallucination is one of the important factors in measuring how much a large language model is trustworthy and reliable. Measuring hallucination on the other hand is also not easy as it seems because each fact can be written in different styles and even the smallest changes in writing make it hard to detect.
HaluEval is one of the datasets that aims to measure hallucination in this field [205]. Evaluation can also be performed by another model judging the response with regard to the actual answer [206].
